In 1513, an Ottoman admiral and geographer compiled a map of the Atlantic world on gazelle skin, drawing — by his own written account — on approximately twenty source maps, including charts he claimed had been made by Christopher Columbus himself. The man, known to posterity by his honorific title rather than his birth name, was a distinguished naval commander who would later write a celebrated compendium of seamanship. His map, now held in Istanbul's Topkapi Palace, showed the coastlines of Europe, Africa, and the Americas with remarkable accuracy for its era.
But a third coastline in the southernmost portion of the map has generated centuries of controversy. A long, curving landmass stretches eastward below the tip of South America. The official record holds that Antarctica was first sighted by European explorers in 1820 — over three centuries after this map was drawn. Proponents of alternative history have cited this as evidence of lost civilisations, advanced pre-Columbian seafaring, or stranger explanations still.
The more sober interpretation is that the coastline represents the theoretical "Terra Australis Incognita" — a speculative southern continent that ancient Greek philosophers had long argued must exist to balance the landmass of the northern hemisphere.
What is this map called, and what is the name of its creator — the Ottoman admiral who compiled it in 1513?
